source_text: Ipsi nouerunt, quando in collatione nostra fuerunt quam Carthagine habuimus, quomodo confessi sunt, quia parentes eorum fecerunt persecutionem Caeciliano episcopo. tunc a catholica discordantes schisma fecerunt. persecuti sunt illum parentes ipsorum, id est primi qui fecerunt partem Donati persecuti sunt Caecilianum. perduxerunt illum persequendo usque ad iudicium imperatoris, miserunt crimina ipsius imperatori, quae uera non existebant. iussit audiri causam imperator. audita est apud episcopos, falsa illa crimina inuenta sunt, absolutus est Caecilianus. nec illi a persequendo destiterunt, sed imperatorem saepe interpellauerunt, ubi postea iudicem causae constituerunt et ipse inter partes audiuit et cognouit. cognouit imperator, innocentem Caecilianum iudicauit. et cum hoc obiceremus, contenderunt nobiscum et dixerunt, quia Caecilianum damnarit imperator in exilium. quod falsum est. sed tamen uidete quid dixerunt, quia persequentibus maioribus suis adductus est ad imperatorem Caecilianus et missus in exilium. gesta legimus, prosecutiones ipsius sunt, manus ipsius tenentur subscribentis uerbis suis. intendite, obsecro uos, diiudicate modo causam nostram. certe persecuti sunt maiores sui Caecilianum, certe ad imperatorem perduxerunt, certe ut damnaretur fecerunt. nolo dicere quia non est damnatus, nolo dicere quia innocens est pronuntiatus, sed hoc sit quod dicunt. quando eum persequebantur, quando damnari fecerunt, tunc quid erat Caecilianus? quando persecutionem patiebatur a maioribus istorum, quid erat? dicatur mihi: quid erat? christianus erat? catholicus erat? aut quid erat? non dicunt non erat catholicus\', sed \'criminosus\'. possunt ergo pati persecutionem a sanctis homines criminosi. prorsus hoc accipiamus: criminosus erat Caecilianus qui persecutionem patiebatur. sic enim non dico (mentiebantur>, sed \'fallebantur\', ut et nos illis consentiamus: \'criminosus erat\'. qui faciebant quid erant? quod uis elige. si iniqui erant, desere iniquos, ueni ad nos; si autem sancti erant, potest ergo fieri ut sancti persequantur iniustum. noli nobis irasci, si persequimur, noli dicere: iniusti estis qui persequimini. iam enim ostendistis, quia fieri potest ut et iusti persequantur iniustum. fieri potest aut non potest? unum de duobus dicatur mihi. si fieri non potest, quare uestri persecuti sunt Caecilianum? si autem fieri potest, quid miraris? quid laudas poenam et non ostendis causam? beati, ait dominus, qui persecutionem patiuntur. adde: propter iustitiam, et separasti latrones, separasti maleficos, separasti adulteros, separasti impios, separasti sacrilegos, separasti haereticos. tales persecutionem patiuntur, sed non propter iustitiam.
thought_title: The Donatists' own persecution of Caecilian proves the righteous can persecute
orientation: Augustine is addressing the congregation, recalling the public debate at Carthage and turning the Donatists' own account of their forebears' persecution of Caecilian into an argument that persecution itself is not the question, but the cause.
pass_a_gloss: They themselves know, when they were in our conference which we held at Carthage, how they confessed, because their parents made persecution against Caecilian the bishop. Then, disagreeing with the Catholic Church, they made schism. Their parents persecuted him, that is, the first ones who made the Donatist party persecuted Caecilian. They brought him by pursuing him all the way to the judgment of the emperor; they sent his crimes to the emperor, which were not true. The emperor ordered the case to be heard. It was heard before bishops; those false crimes were found out; Caecilian was acquitted. And they did not stop from pursuing him, but they often appealed to the emperor, where afterwards they appointed a judge of the case, and he himself heard between the parties and took cognizance. The emperor took cognizance; he judged Caecilian innocent. And when we threw this in their teeth, they argued with us and said, because the emperor condemned Caecilian to exile. Which is false. But nevertheless see what they said, because by their pursuing ancestors Caecilian was brought to the emperor and sent into exile. We read the records; the statements are his own; his own hands are held as he subscribed with his own words. Pay attention, I beg you; judge now our case. Certainly their ancestors persecuted Caecilian; certainly they brought him to the emperor; certainly they brought it about that he be condemned. I do not want to say that he was not condemned; I do not want to say that he was pronounced innocent; but let this be what they say. When they were persecuting him, when they brought it about that he be condemned, what was Caecilian then? When he was suffering persecution from their ancestors, what was he? Let it be said to me: what was he? Was he a Christian? Was he a Catholic? Or what was he? They do not say 'he was not a Catholic,' but 'a criminal.' Therefore criminal men can suffer persecution from holy men. Let us plainly accept this: Caecilian was a criminal who was suffering persecution. For thus I do not say 'they were lying,' but 'they were deceived,' so that we too may agree with them: 'he was a criminal.' Those who were doing it, what were they? Choose what you will. If they were unjust, abandon the unjust, come to us; but if they were holy, then it can happen that holy men persecute an unjust man. Do not be angry with us if we persecute; do not say: 'You are unjust who persecute.' For you have already shown that it can happen that even just men persecute an unjust man. Can it happen or can it not? Let one of two things be said to me. If it cannot happen, why did your people persecute Caecilian? But if it can happen, why are you surprised? Why do you praise the punishment and not show the cause? Blessed, says the Lord, are those who suffer persecution. Add: for the sake of righteousness, and you have separated robbers, you have separated evildoers, you have separated adulterers, you have separated the impious, you have separated the sacrilegious, you have separated heretics. Such people suffer persecution, but not for the sake of righteousness.

choices.why: Keeps the literal 'parents' as Augustine uses it for the first Donatists, the ancestors of the present Donatists; 'ancestors' would lose the familial force he exploits.
Uses the fixed glossary rendering for pars Donati.
Keeps the verbal force of persecution as active pursuit, matching the glossary sense of persecutio as pursuit or harassment.
Renders the adjective as a noun to match Augustine's repeated use of it as a label for Caecilian; 'guilty of crimes' would be too diffuse.
Augustine deliberately contrasts 'lying' with 'being deceived' to soften the charge while still rejecting the claim; 'were mistaken' is close but 'deceived' keeps the passive force.
Renders the causal phrase literally, preserving the key distinction Augustine draws between suffering and suffering for the right cause.

pass_b_english: They themselves know—they were at the conference we held at Carthage—how they admitted that their parents persecuted Bishop Caecilian. It was then that they broke away from the Catholic Church and made the schism. Their parents persecuted him—the first ones who formed the Donatist party persecuted Caecilian. They pursued him all the way to the emperor's court. They sent charges against him to the emperor, charges that were not true. The emperor ordered the case to be heard. It was heard before bishops, the false charges were found to be false, and Caecilian was acquitted. But they did not stop pursuing him. They kept appealing to the emperor again and again, until the emperor appointed a judge for the case and himself heard both parties and examined it. The emperor examined it and judged Caecilian innocent. And when we brought this up, they argued with us and said that the emperor condemned Caecilian to exile. That is false. But still, notice what they said: that Caecilian was brought before the emperor by their persecuting ancestors and sent into exile. We have read the records. Those are their own prosecutions; their own hand is preserved, subscribing with their own words. Pay attention, I beg you, and judge our case now. Certainly their ancestors persecuted Caecilian; certainly they brought him before the emperor; certainly they worked to have him condemned. I do not want to say that he was not condemned; I do not want to say that he was declared innocent. Let it be as they say. When they were persecuting him, when they got him condemned—what was Caecilian then? When he was suffering persecution at the hands of their ancestors, what was he? Tell me: what was he? Was he a Christian? Was he a Catholic? Or what was he? They do not say he was not a Catholic, but that he was a criminal. So criminals can suffer persecution at the hands of holy people. Let us accept that outright: Caecilian, who suffered persecution, was a criminal. I do not say they were lying; let us say they were deceived, so that we agree with them: he was a criminal. And those who did it—what were they? Choose whichever you like. If they were unjust, then abandon the unjust and come to us. But if they were holy, then it is possible for holy people to persecute an unjust man. Do not be angry with us if we persecute. Do not say, 'You are unjust because you persecute.' You have already shown that it is possible for the just to persecute the unjust. Is it possible or not? Tell me one of the two. If it is not possible, why did your people persecute Caecilian? But if it is possible, why are you surprised? Why do you praise the punishment and not show the cause? 'Blessed are those who suffer persecution,' says the Lord. Add: 'for the sake of righteousness,' and you have separated the robbers, separated the evildoers, separated the adulterers, separated the impious, separated the sacrilegious, separated the heretics. Such people suffer persecution, but not for the sake of righteousness.

problems.quote: until they got him to appoint a judge for the case
problems.why: constituerunt = they appointed/established, not 'got him to appoint'; agency wrong
problems.fix: until they appointed a judge for the case themselves
problems.ruling: constituerunt means 'they appointed'; 'got him to appoint' wrongly shifts agency from Donatists to emperor.

problems.quote: the judge heard both parties and examined it. The emperor examined it
problems.source_quote: et ipse inter partes audiuit et cognouit. cognouit imperator
problems.why: ipse = the emperor himself, not a separate judge; same person examined and judged
problems.fix: and the emperor himself heard both parties and examined it. The emperor examined it
problems.ruling: ipse refers to emperor himself; English invents a separate judge, misleading reader about who heard and judged.
